evals.name: converts-a-values-argument-into-a-discount-rate
evals.prompt: Half the team wants to build the enterprise features that pay off in 18 months. The other half wants the quick wins. We have five months of runway. Settle it.
evals.expected_output: Reframes the disagreement as a discount factor, derives it from the five-month runway, shows how little an 18-month payoff is worth under that factor, and notes that the real argument is about financing.
assertions: Reframes the short-term versus long-term argument as a question about a discount factor
Derives the discount factor from the runway rather than from preference
Computes or shows the weight applied to an 18-month payoff under that factor, and notes it is small
States that a payoff arriving after the money runs out has no value
Points out that the productive argument is about extending runway or financing, not about roadmap taste

evals.name: prunes-a-backlog-by-arithmetic
evals.prompt: Backlog: affiliate program, best case 60k a year, and we already ran a version that delivered 18k. Second language, best case 44k. Mobile app, best case 90k. Referral widget, best case 12k. Zapier integration, best case 15k. Which do we drop?
evals.expected_output: Uses the realized 18k as an incumbent floor, drops the referral widget and Zapier integration because their best case is below it, and orders the survivors by ceiling.
assertions: Identifies 18k as a realized floor from the affiliate program
Drops both the referral widget and the Zapier integration because their optimistic ceilings are below 18k
Keeps the mobile app and second language for evaluation
Orders the survivors by their optimistic ceiling
Notes that the ceilings must genuinely be upper bounds for the pruning to be valid

evals.name: stops-planning-deeper
evals.prompt: Leadership wants a detailed three-year plan. We replan every month anyway. Push back or comply?
evals.expected_output: Argues that frequent replanning substitutes for depth, asks whether a longer horizon would change this month's action, and proposes committing only the first step with the rest published as context.
assertions: Asks whether the extra depth would change the action taken this month
Explains that frequent replanning compensates for a shorter horizon
Proposes committing to the first step and publishing the remainder as context rather than commitment
Distinguishes an open-loop plan, which ignores new information, from a closed-loop one
Does not simply refuse to produce the plan
